Chapter 28 Non-Alcoholic Cocktails – Dining Room & Beverage Management for Culinary Students

## LEARNING OBJECTIVES After completing this chapter, students will be able to: * Create sophisticated non-alcoholic cocktails that rival alcoholic versions in complexity * Understand techniques for building flavor, balance, and interest without spirits * Identify and use ingredients that add depth and character to non-alcoholic drinks * Develop non-alcoholic beverage programs that serve diverse guest needs * Apply cocktail principles to non-alcoholic drink creation * Recognize and avoid common pitfalls in mocktail development * Price and present non-alcoholic cocktails appropriately * Serve guests who abstain from alcohol with the same care as those who drink * * * ## KEY TERMS Mocktail: A non-alcoholic cocktail, though the term is increasingly considered dismissive; “non-alcoholic cocktail” or “zero-proof cocktail” are preferred. Zero-proof: Containing no alcohol, used to describe spirits substitutes, cocktails, or beverage programs. Seedlip: A pioneering non-alcoholic distilled spirit brand that helped establish the zero-proof spirits category. Shrub: A drinking vinegar made from fruit, sugar, and vinegar, providing acidity and complexity in cocktails. Kombucha: Fermented tea with natural effervescence and complex flavor, useful in non-alcoholic drinks for its tang and depth. Aquafaba: The liquid from cooked chickpeas, used as a vegan egg white substitute in cocktails for foam and texture. Bitters: Aromatic flavoring agents typically containing alcohol but used in small enough quantities that drinks remain essentially non-alcoholic when bitters are the only alcohol source. Tonic: A carbonated beverage originally containing quinine, now available in craft versions with complex botanical flavors beyond commercial tonic water. Cordial: A concentrated sweetened syrup, often fruit or herb based, diluted to create drinks. Botanical: Plant-based ingredients including herbs, spices, flowers, or roots that add aromatic complexity to drinks. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ ## THE EVOLUTION OF NON-ALCOHOLIC DRINKING For decades, guests who didn’t drink alcohol faced dismal choices: soda, juice, or water. Restaurants and bars treated non-alcoholic options as afterthoughts, offering nothing that approached the sophistication, complexity, or craft of their alcoholic cocktail programs. This neglect reflected an assumption that guests not drinking alcohol were unimportant or that sophisticated non-alcoholic drinks were impossible or unnecessary. This has changed dramatically in recent years. Growing awareness of alcohol’s health impacts, changing social attitudes toward drinking, religious and cultural considerations, increased health consciousness, and simple personal preference have created substantial demand for sophisticated non-alcoholic options. The global “sober curious” movement—people choosing to reduce or eliminate alcohol consumption without identifying as abstinent—has accelerated this trend, creating a market for drinks that provide cocktail experience without alcohol. The emergence of quality zero-proof spirits, sophisticated mixers, and innovative techniques has made truly excellent non-alcoholic cocktails possible. Brands like Seedlip, Lyre’s, and Ritual produce non-alcoholic spirits that credibly approximate gin, whiskey, or rum. Craft tonic waters, shrubs, drinking vinegars, and botanical syrups provide complexity that cheap mixers never could. Bartenders applying cocktail craft to non-alcoholic drinks create beverages that satisfy as completely as their alcoholic counterparts. Professional beverage programs increasingly treat non-alcoholic cocktails as equals to alcoholic ones, pricing them appropriately for effort and ingredients, presenting them with equal care, and developing them with the same attention to balance and complexity. This evolution reflects both business opportunity and ethical responsibility—every guest deserves quality beverage options regardless of whether they drink alcohol. Understanding that guests abstain from alcohol for diverse reasons helps you serve them appropriately. Some are recovering from addiction and find alcohol’s presence triggering. Some have religious or cultural prohibitions. Some are pregnant or nursing. Some have health conditions incompatible with alcohol. Some are designated drivers. Some simply don’t enjoy alcohol. Each context requires sensitivity, and all deserve the same quality service and options as guests drinking alcohol. * * * ## PRINCIPLES OF NON-ALCOHOLIC COCKTAIL CREATION Creating excellent non-alcoholic cocktails requires understanding what spirits contribute beyond alcohol and how to achieve similar effects through alternative means. Spirits provide not just intoxication but also flavor, aromatic complexity, body, bitterness, and mouthfeel. Removing alcohol without replacing these elements produces thin, sweet, simple drinks that fail to satisfy. ## **Building Complexity** Complexity in cocktails comes from layering multiple flavors that interact harmoniously. Alcoholic cocktails achieve this through spirits with inherent complexity, modifiers like vermouth or liqueurs, and aromatic elements like bitters. Non-alcoholic versions must create similar complexity through other means. Multiple juices or purees create layered fruit flavors rather than single-note sweetness. Combining apple, pear, and lemon juice produces more interest than apple juice alone. Herb infusions or botanical teas add aromatic depth. Spices like ginger, cardamom, or cinnamon contribute warming complexity. Fermented ingredients like kombucha or shrubs bring acidity and funk. The goal is building drinks with multiple flavor dimensions rather than simple, one-dimensional sweetness. ### **Balancing Sweet and Tart** The sweet-tart balance fundamental to cocktails applies equally to non-alcoholic drinks. Many failed mocktails are simply too sweet, relying on juice or sweet syrups without sufficient acidity to balance them. Incorporating citrus juices, shrubs, drinking vinegars, or tart kombucha creates balance that makes drinks refreshing rather than cloying. The classic sour ratio (2:1:1 spirit, citrus, sweetener) provides a starting template, but the “spirit” portion requires replacement with something providing substance. This might be tea, juice, zero-proof spirit, or a combination creating sufficient body and flavor to anchor the drink. ### **Adding Body and Texture** Spirits provide viscosity and mouthfeel that water or juice alone cannot match. Creating appropriate body in non-alcoholic drinks requires ingredients that add texture without excessive sweetness or thickness. Options include: Syrups made with rich ratios (2:1 sugar to water) rather than simple syrup (1:1) contribute more body. Nut milks or coconut cream add creamy texture and fat that creates richness. Aquafaba provides texture and foam similar to egg whites when shaken vigorously. Muddled fruit adds pulp and texture. Carbonation creates mouthfeel and lightness that suggests complexity. ### **Incorporating Bitterness and Aromatics** Bitterness balances sweetness and adds sophistication to drinks. While bitters contain alcohol, the tiny amounts used (a few dashes) contribute negligible alcohol content while providing aromatic complexity. Many bartenders include bitters in “non-alcoholic” drinks, though some guests avoiding alcohol completely cannot accept this, requiring alternatives. Non-alcoholic bitters exist (Fee Brothers makes several), providing aromatic complexity without alcohol. Teas, particularly black or pu-erh, contribute tannin and bitterness. Tonic water adds quinine bitterness. Grapefruit juice or peel provides pleasant bitterness. These elements prevent drinks from tasting one-dimensionally sweet. ### **Using Zero-Proof Spirits** Non-alcoholic spirits have evolved from curiosities to legitimate ingredients. These products use distillation, maceration, or blending to create flavors approximating gin, whiskey, rum, or other spirits without alcohol. Quality varies enormously—some are impressive while others taste medicinal or artificial—but the best provide solid foundations for non-alcoholic cocktails. Using zero-proof spirits follows the same principles as using regular spirits: they provide base flavor and structure, modified with mixers, citrus, and aromatic elements. A non-alcoholic gin and tonic made with quality zero-proof gin, craft tonic, fresh lime, and proper ice rivals the alcoholic version. A non-alcoholic old fashioned using zero-proof whiskey alternative can be genuinely satisfying. * * * ## ESSENTIAL INGREDIENTS FOR NON-ALCOHOLIC COCKTAILS Developing excellent non-alcoholic programs requires stocking ingredients that build complexity and interest beyond what standard bar inventories provide. ### **Shrubs and Drinking Vinegars** Shrubs combine fruit, sugar, and vinegar, creating concentrated syrups with bright acidity and complex fruit flavors. The vinegar provides tartness similar to citrus but with different character—deeper, more complex, sometimes funky. Shrubs mixed with soda water create interesting drinks on their own or combine with other ingredients in more complex cocktails. Making shrubs is straightforward: macerate fruit with sugar (typically equal weights), allow to sit for several hours or days as sugar draws out juice, strain, then add vinegar (typically cider vinegar or white wine vinegar) to taste. The resulting syrup is intensely flavored and acidic, used in small quantities to flavor drinks. ### **Kombucha** Kombucha’s fermentation creates natural carbonation, complex flavors, and pleasant acidity that works beautifully in cocktails. Using kombucha as a base or modifier adds depth that simple sodas cannot match. The slight funk from fermentation creates character similar to wine or barrel-aged spirits, and the carbonation provides textural interest. Various kombucha flavors exist—from plain black tea fermentation to fruit or herb infused versions—each bringing distinct character. Ginger kombucha adds spice and acidity, berry kombuchas contribute fruit complexity, and plain kombucha provides a neutral acidic and carbonated base. ### **Botanical Syrups and Infusions** Creating house-made syrups infused with herbs, spices, flowers, or teas produces ingredients with genuine complexity. Lavender syrup, rosemary honey syrup, ginger-cardamom syrup, or jasmine tea syrup all contribute aromatic depth that elevates drinks beyond simple sweeteners. These syrups require minimal effort—steep botanical ingredients in hot simple syrup, strain when desired flavor develops, bottle, and refrigerate. They keep for weeks and transform otherwise simple drinks into sophisticated offerings. ### **Teas and Tisanes** Tea provides tannin, bitterness, and complex flavors that create substance in non-alcoholic drinks. Green tea offers fresh, vegetal character. Black tea contributes robustness and tannin. Oolong provides floral or fruity notes. Herbal tisanes like hibiscus (tart and fruity) or rooibos (naturally sweet and smooth) create diverse flavor profiles. Cold-brewed tea works particularly well in cocktails, producing smoother, less bitter infusions than hot-brewed tea. Strong tea (double or triple normal concentration) provides sufficient intensity to register in mixed drinks. ### **Craft Sodas and Tonics** Commercial sodas and tonics are designed for mass appeal, emphasizing sweetness over complexity. Craft alternatives offer actual botanical complexity, appropriate sweetness, and quality carbonation. Fever-Tree tonic, Q tonic, and similar brands dramatically improve any drink using tonic. Artisanal ginger beers provide real ginger spice rather than artificial flavoring. Making house sodas from syrups and carbonated water allows complete control over sweetness and flavor, creating sodas that precisely match your needs rather than accepting commercial compromises. ### **Verjus** Verjus, the pressed juice of unripe grapes, provides wine-like acidity and subtle fruit character without alcohol. It works beautifully as a modifier in non-alcoholic cocktails, contributing complexity and acidity that bridges fruit juices and alcohols. Verjus is relatively expensive and may be hard to source, but its unique character makes it valuable for sophisticated non-alcoholic drinks. ### **Fresh Juices and Purees** Fresh juices remain fundamental to quality drinks, alcoholic or not. Beyond citrus, consider fresh apple juice (pressed, not from concentrate), pear juice, grape juice, watermelon juice, or cucumber juice. Each provides distinct flavor and can be combined for complexity. Fruit purees—raspberry, passion fruit, mango—add concentrated flavor and texture. Using small amounts prevents excessive sweetness while providing intense fruit character. * * * ## CLASSIC MOCKTAIL FORMULAS AND VARIATIONS Several established non-alcoholic drinks provide templates for development and variations. ### **Virgin Mojito** The non-alcoholic mojito demonstrates how removing rum while maintaining other elements creates a satisfying drink. Fresh mint, lime juice, sugar, and soda water combine for refreshing complexity. The key is generous mint—eight to ten leaves—muddled gently to release oils without shredding, and proper balance between lime acidity and sugar sweetness. Variations might add fruit (strawberry, raspberry), substitute honey for sugar, or include cucumber for additional freshness. The template of muddled herbs, citrus, sweetener, and soda creates countless possibilities. ### **Shirley Temple / Roy Rogers** These children’s drinks are often dismissed but demonstrate functional formulas: ginger ale or lemon-lime soda plus grenadine, garnished with cherries and orange. While overly sweet as typically made, the template of soda plus flavored syrup plus fruit garnish works when proportions are adjusted and quality ingredients used. Using craft ginger beer, house-made grenadine (pomegranate juice reduced with sugar rather than corn syrup and artificial flavoring), and fresh fruit creates an adult version that’s genuinely enjoyable. ### **Arnold Palmer** Half iced tea, half lemonade creates this golf-course classic. The combination balances tea’s tannin with lemonade’s sweet-tart brightness. Quality versions use fresh-brewed tea and house-made lemonade rather than commercial sweet tea and lemon juice from concentrate. Variations include using different teas (green tea, peach tea, hibiscus), adjusting the ratio, or adding fresh herbs like mint or basil. The simplicity makes it reliable while allowing creative modifications. ### **Italian Sodas** Italian sodas combine flavored syrup with soda water, sometimes with cream creating a “cream soda.” Using quality syrups (fruit purees, botanical infusions, or house-made flavored syrups) rather than artificial flavorings creates sophisticated drinks. Adding cream or coconut cream provides richness that makes these feel substantial. * * * ## ORIGINAL NON-ALCOHOLIC COCKTAIL DEVELOPMENT Creating original non-alcoholic cocktails follows the same principles as alcoholic cocktail development: understanding balance, working within proven structures, testing and refining, and seeking feedback. ### **Template-Based Development** Using classic cocktail templates with non-alcoholic substitutions provides reliable starting points. A sour template (2 parts base, 1 part citrus, 1 part sweetener) works whether the base is rum or kombucha. An Old Fashioned template (spirit, sugar, bitters, water) functions with zero-proof whiskey as well as bourbon. Consider what the original cocktail provides and how to replicate it without alcohol. A Margarita provides tequila’s agave character, lime’s brightness, and orange liqueur’s sweetness and citrus. A non-alcoholic version might use agave nectar for sweetness and agave character, lime juice for acidity, and orange juice or orange bitters for citrus complexity. ### **Seasonal Development** Seasonal ingredients inspire non-alcoholic cocktails as readily as alcoholic ones. Summer strawberries, spring rhubarb, fall apples, winter citrus—each season offers ingredients that create distinctive drinks. Using seasonal produce at peak quality ensures maximum flavor and creates variety across the year. ### **Texture and Presentation** Since non-alcoholic cocktails can’t rely on alcohol’s effects to satisfy guests, presentation and texture matter even more. Creating foam with aquafaba, layering ingredients for visual interest, using dramatic garnishes, or serving drinks smoking with dry ice (if safe protocols are followed) adds theater that enhances the experience. Glassware selection also matters. Serving non-alcoholic cocktails in appropriate cocktail glassware—coupes, rocks glasses, highball glasses—signals that these drinks deserve the same respect as alcoholic cocktails. Plastic cups or casual glassware undermines the sophistication you’re trying to create. * * * ## MENU DEVELOPMENT AND PROGRAM DESIGN Incorporating non-alcoholic cocktails into your program requires thoughtful menu design, staff training, and operational consideration. ### **Menu Placement and Presentation** Some establishments create separate non-alcoholic cocktail sections on menus, while others integrate non-alcoholic options throughout. Both approaches work, though separate sections make options more visible to guests seeking them while integration normalizes non-alcoholic drinking. Avoid calling these drinks “mocktails”—the term diminishes them and sounds juvenile. Use “non-alcoholic cocktails,” “zero-proof cocktails,” or simply list them alongside alcoholic options without special designation. Describe them with the same attention to flavor and character you give alcoholic drinks. ### **Pricing Strategy** Pricing non-alcoholic cocktails causes debate. Some argue they should cost significantly less than alcoholic versions since spirits are the most expensive ingredients. Others argue that effort, other ingredients, and time justify pricing comparable to alcoholic cocktails. The best approach prices based on ingredient cost, effort, and value provided. A complex non-alcoholic cocktail using multiple juices, house-made syrups, and careful preparation deserves appropriate pricing—perhaps $8-12 if alcoholic cocktails run $12-15. A simple virgin mojito might be priced lower at $6-8. The key is ensuring price reflects value while not undervaluing non-alcoholic options. ### **Staff Training** Ensure all staff understand non-alcoholic offerings and can describe them enthusiastically. Servers should suggest non-alcoholic cocktails as naturally as alcoholic ones, without making guests feel defensive about not drinking alcohol. “Would you like to see our cocktail menu? We have both alcoholic and non-alcoholic options” frames choice neutrally. Train bartenders in proper non-alcoholic cocktail execution. These drinks deserve the same technique and care as alcoholic cocktails—proper shaking, correct dilution, appropriate garnish, clean presentation. Sloppy execution undermines the program regardless of recipe quality. ### **Offering Modifications** Many alcoholic cocktails can be modified to non-alcoholic versions by substituting zero-proof spirits or removing alcohol while adjusting other ingredients to maintain balance. Training staff to suggest these modifications expands options beyond the listed non-alcoholic menu. However, not every cocktail translates well. Spirit-forward cocktails like Manhattans or Martinis lose their essential character when alcohol is removed, even with zero-proof substitutions. Be honest about which drinks work well in non-alcoholic versions and which don’t, steering guests toward better options rather than disappointing them with inferior substitutions. * * * ## SERVING DIVERSE ABSTINENCE CONTEXTS Understanding why guests abstain helps you serve them appropriately and sensitively. ### **Health and Wellness** Many guests reduce or eliminate alcohol for health reasons—medication interactions, weight management, liver health, sleep quality, or general wellness. These guests often appreciate sophisticated alternatives that allow social participation without alcohol. They typically don’t mind being around alcohol and may be comfortable with trace amounts from bitters. ### **Recovery and Sobriety** Guests in recovery from addiction require different consideration. They may find bar environments triggering and appreciate acknowledgment of their sobriety. Some cannot accept any alcohol, even trace amounts from bitters. Some prefer drinks that don’t resemble alcoholic cocktails, finding mimicry uncomfortable. Sensitivity to their needs while providing quality options serves them well. Never pressure guests to explain why they’re not drinking. Accept “I’m not drinking tonight” without question or comment. Never express disappointment or try to convince them to drink. Your role is supporting their choices, not judging or influencing them. ### **Religious and Cultural Considerations** Various religions prohibit alcohol—Islam, some Christian denominations, certain Buddhist traditions. Cultural considerations may also influence drinking choices. These guests appreciate quality alternatives that allow full participation in social occasions without compromising beliefs. ### **Pregnancy and Medical Conditions** Pregnant or nursing guests require complete alcohol avoidance. Guests with certain medical conditions or taking specific medications cannot safely consume alcohol. Both groups deserve quality alternatives without needing to explain their situations. ### **Designated Drivers** Designated drivers perform valuable service by enabling others to drink safely. They deserve appreciation through quality non-alcoholic options, perhaps offered complimentary or at reduced prices as thanks for their responsibility. * * * **PRACTICAL EXERCISE**: NON-ALCOHOLIC COCKTAIL MASTERY These exercises develop skills in creating and serving sophisticated non-alcoholic cocktails. **Exercise 1: Building Complexity Comparison** Create two non-alcoholic drinks: one using only single-source ingredients (orange juice and simple syrup, for example), another using multiple ingredients for complexity (apple juice, pear juice, lemon juice, ginger syrup, muddled mint). Taste both and identify how layering creates interest versus single-source simplicity. **Exercise 2: Zero-Proof Spirit Evaluation** Obtain several zero-proof spirits (non-alcoholic gin, whiskey, or rum alternatives). Taste each neat, then use them in simple serves (with tonic, in a sour formula, in an old fashioned template). Evaluate which products work well and which fail to deliver, understanding quality differences within the category. **Exercise 3: Shrub Creation and Application** Make a fruit shrub from scratch: macerate berries with sugar, strain, add vinegar. Use the shrub in multiple applications: diluted with soda water, as a modifier in a complex cocktail, or mixed with kombucha. Document how shrubs contribute acidity and complexity. **Exercise 4: Original Non-Alcoholic Cocktail Development** Develop three original non-alcoholic cocktails using different templates: one riff on a classic cocktail structure, one seasonal drink featuring peak ingredients, one using zero-proof spirits as a base. Test and refine each, seeking feedback from diverse tasters. Present final recipes with full specs, descriptions, and reasoning for ingredient choices. **Exercise 5: Mocktail vs. Sophisticated Non-Alcoholic Comparison** Create two drinks: one stereotypical mocktail (overly sweet, simple, using commercial mixers), one sophisticated non-alcoholic cocktail (properly balanced, complex, using quality ingredients). Taste both and analyze the dramatic difference in quality and satisfaction. This exercise reinforces why technique and ingredients matter as much for non-alcoholic drinks as alcoholic ones. **Exercise 6: Service Sensitivity Training** Role-play various scenarios involving guests not drinking alcohol: someone in recovery, a pregnant guest, a designated driver, someone who simply doesn’t drink. Practice offering options, describing drinks, and handling service without making guests uncomfortable or pressured to explain their choices. Develop sensitivity to the diverse reasons people abstain and appropriate responses for each context. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ ## REVIEW QUESTIONS 1. Describe three techniques for adding body and texture to non-alcoholic cocktails that might otherwise taste thin. 7. Going alcohol-free? Pregnant? Sober? Whatever the reason, here is your ultimate guide to non-alcoholic mocktails, including recipes. Learn more at A Bar Above.

## Mocktails for Dry January & Beyond

Obviously, we at A Bar Above love cocktails, beer, and wine. BUT taking a break from alcohol for a Dry January (or any other month) can be so beneficial whether your goal is resetting habits, weight loss, or even better sleep.

Part of pouring craft beverages is the process of discovering, developing, and sharing tasty sips with our friends and family. And on that note, “without alcohol” _doesn’t_ have to signal the end of delicious and the beginning of boring. This guide to craft mocktails will deliver all of the flavor and flair of cocktails while helping you keep your commitment to [#DryJanuary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dry_January).

Plus, for those in the hospitality industry, offering thoughtfully crafted non-alcoholic choices for guests who are not drinking alcohol– for whatever reason– is just excellent service and good for business.

## What is a Craft Mocktail?

By now, we have all learned that “mocktail” means a non-alcoholic drink meant to replicate a cocktail. But surprisingly, the [Journal of American Speech](https://www.jstor.org/stable/455331) notes the [origin word “mocktail”](https://preventionconversation.org/2017/10/30/who-coined-the-term-mocktail-anyway-2/) doesn’t come from a sober mixologist but instead a 1979 Libbey Glass advertisement. Random, right?

Just as cocktails have moved to the classic hand-shaken Daiquiri, so have we moved beyond the virgin blender drink. Today, we see a wide variety of non-alcoholic options under bar menu headings that include Zero ABV, Low & No Alcohol, Alcohol-Free, NA Options, and Zero Proof.

By whatever name you call them, really good craft mocktails require care, skill, and fresh ingredients, just like their boozy cousins. In short, they should be as well-crafted as a cocktail.

## Trends in Alcohol-Free

At one time, not drinking– whether you were the designated driver, sober, pregnant, or simply abstaining– meant getting to select from sugary soda, juice, tonic, lousy coffee, or tap water. _Not very appealing options._

The “big upgrade” to this list was the addition of non-alcoholic beer.

However, today, as reflected in the[2020 Cocktail Trends Report](https://www.beveragedaily.com/Article/2020/03/02/Bacardi-Going-back-to-the-bar-helps-us-look-forward-to-cocktail-trends), the #1 trend is low/no alcohol drinks. The craft mocktail is a rising star due to more mindful drinking and hospitality professionals serving up what their guests want.

What gets measured gets improved, and the mocktail is no exception. If you are in doubt, consider this:

*   Alcohol-free – sober bars are popping up [around the world](https://www.bbc.com/worklife/article/20190510-can-you-have-any-fun-at-a-bar-with-no-booze) and [in the US](https://www.smartbrief.com/original/2020/05/nonalcoholic-drink-trend-shows-no-sign-slowing-down).
*   [Non-alcoholic bar programs](https://www.themanual.com/food-and-drink/best-sober-friendly-bars/) are getting the attention previously reserved only for craft cocktails.
*   [Zero proof spirits](https://www.winemag.com/2020/01/14/12-best-non-alcoholic-spirits/) are being produced, marketed, and added to the back bar next to the classics.
*   DIY mocktail books abound, such as the famed Aviary Restaurant’s [_Zero, A New Approach to Non-Alcoholic Drinks_](https://www.theaviarybook.com/zero-standard-edition/).

_But enough talk. Let’s make some mocktails!_

## Getting Started Making Craft Mocktails

My [three principles of “craft”](https://abarabove.com/what-is-craft/) apply to both cocktails and mocktails. It can be challenging, but with a little bit of practice, you’ll be an excellent mocktail mixologist.

### **#1: Care**

Give serious consideration to the non-alcoholic beverage you’re creating. Who will be drinking it and when? This includes the food that will complement the experience.

*   **Who:**Do they abstain from alcohol entirely, or can you use dashes of bitters, which will add a tiny amount of alcohol?
*   **When:**What’s the occasion and setting? The “who” and “when” answers will influence the glass, temperature, and the flavors and textures desired. Remember, the drink’s glass and size should match the alcoholic counterpart, as not to draw attention to the person who isn’t drinking alcohol.

![Image 1: bartender shaking a cocktail in a cocktail shaker](blob:http://localhost/0262c578668d739527842d85ccf8e004)

Copyright A Bar Above

### **#2: Skill**

Your objective is to mix a flavorful, complex, balanced, and beautiful drink.

*   **Flavorful:**The drink should have a distinct flavor, not a watered-down juice or weak hint of something added to soda water.
*   **Complex:**Complexity will come from using various flavors and aromas that blend harmoniously or provide an exciting contrast.
*   **Balance:**Balance is the interplay between the five basic taste elements: sweet, salty, sour, bitter, and umami. A well-balanced drink will use multiple ingredients in proportion so that a single flavor does not leave the drink tasting one-dimensional.
*   **Beauty** – We eat and drink with our eyes first. Use garnishes, ice, and glassware to create flair and enhance the experience of the drink you are making.

![Image 2: Fresh juice in mugs on a countertop](blob:http://localhost/f48b1e80ee7e6beb4b7dfe4f3f4aa680)

Photo via www.unsplash.com

### **#3: Fresh Ingredients**

The craft cocktail movement is founded on the use of fresh juices, house-made syrups, shrubs, tinctures, fresh-picked herbs and flowers, and the use of artisan brands. So, too, are craft mocktails**.**

*   **Juice:** A handheld or electric juicer may become part of your essential bar equipment.
*   **Syrups**, **Shrubs, and Tinctures:** These not only provide sweetness but also enhance your drinks with tartness, herbs, spices, fruit flavors, and peppers to build balance and complexity.
*   **Fresh-picked:**Both taste and aroma create flavor. The use of fresh herbs and flowers in juices, syrups, and garnishes enhances the flavors you are making while also setting expectations visually.
*   **Artisan:**Whenever possible, choose to make your mocktail ingredients at home or purchase brands that embrace the craft movement’s ethos.

## Inspired Flavors

Aristotle said, “The whole is greater than the sum of its parts.” And that’s totally true with mocktails and cocktails. The interplay between a dash of this and a small amount of that, mixed with something else, can create a flavor profile that is truly inspired.

On that note, these books helped me to understand flavor pairing. I consult them regularly to expand my knowledge of flavor and creativity:

*   [_The Drunken Botanist_, The Plants That Create The World’s Great Drinks](https://drunkenbotanist.com/) by Amy Stewart
*   [_The Flavor Bible_, The Essential Guide to Culinary Creativity, Based On The Wisdom of America’s Most Imaginative Chefs](https://karenandandrew.com/books/the-flavor-bible/)by Karen Page and Andrew Dornenburg

## Craft Mocktail Mixology

Thanks to [Spirity Non-Alcoholic cocktails](https://spiritycocktails.com/) and other similar brands, craft mocktails can be as quick and painless as opening a can– After all, craft beer is still _craft_. Or it can be as involved as making your own zero ABV spirits, developing syrups, and handcrafting bitters at home.

Usually, it falls somewhere in between; I buy some things and make others.

All three options above are perfect depending on the occasion and how much time and equipment you have available.

1.   **Easy and Quick:** This doesn’t have to mean sugary and sweet. Creating a complex, well-balanced, and attractive drink can be as quick as combining bitters, shrubs, or balsamic vinegar with the mixer of your choice, along with a thoughtful garnish.

## Lemongrass and Mint Cooler

*   ¼ – ½ ounce of Lemongrass and Mint White Balsamic Vinegar
*   4 ounces of soda water

Presentation: Pour into a Collins glass with 4 one-inch ice cubes, and garnish with a sprig of fresh mint and a twist of lemon.

## Bitters and Soda

Bitters and soda is a classic non-alcoholic choice. Yes, bitters are generally made by using alcohol to extract flavors from roots, herbs, leaves, and fruit,; but when used in small quantities has no intoxicating effect. In the US, a beverage with less than .5% Alcohol By Volume (ABV) is considered non-alcoholic. There are also [non-alcoholic bitters](https://abarabove.com/non-alcoholic-bitters/) available.

In your local liquor store and online, you’ll find a wide array of bitters. There’s no reason to limit yourself to Angostura Bitters only!

Bitters and soda are also readily available pre-mixed in a can from [Hella](https://hellacocktail.co/pages/bitters-soda), Angostura, and Schweppes, to name a few.

**Bitters and Soda**

*   2 – 6 dashes of bitters
*   4 – 8 ounces of soda water

Presentation: Pour into a pint, rocks, or Collins glass, making sure to match the glassware and portion to the alcoholic drinks served. Garnish with a complementing or contrasting flavor element. The book _Flavor Matrix_ is invaluable for great ideas.

Copyright A Bar Above, generated with AI

## **Tonic Water & Lime**

Readily available and straightforward, this go-to non-alcoholic choice can be full of sugar. Still, with a few upgrades, you can reduce the sugar and increase flavor.

**Elevated Tonic and Lime**

*   4 – 6 ounces of Fever-Tree Tonic
*   3 – 6 dashes of Woodland Bitters from Portland Bitters Project

Presentation: Pour into a large rocks or Collins glass, matching the glassware and portion to the alcoholic drinks served. Garnish with a lime wheel and rosemary sprig.

### **Make Vs. Buy**

This is what craft cocktail enthusiasts and bartenders do most of the time with craft cocktails. We purchase spirits, vermouth, bitters, etc., and then we make syrups, shrubs, and other easy-to-prepare ingredients. _Craft mocktails are no different!_

Today, there are many brands and [choices of spirits when you are stocking your sober bar](https://www.winemag.com/2020/01/14/12-best-non-alcoholic-spirits/). For a deeper dive, check out the [Mixology Talk podcast #177](https://abarabove.com/podcast/mtp177-non-alcoholic-spirits-seedlip-laura-lashley/) as I talk non-alcoholic cocktails with Laura Lashley, a Brand Ambassador for Seedlip.

Ok, so now that the basics are out of the way, let’s dive in by focusing on three non-alcoholic versions of classic cocktails: The Old Fashioned, the Daiquiri, and the Negroni.

## **DIY Mixology**

If you are a total cocktail nerd who is getting into craft mocktails, I highly suggest you order [_Zero, A New Approach to Non-alcoholic Drinks_](https://www.theaviarybook.com/zero-standard-edition/). In it, you’ll find the guidance to make your own zero ABV backbar inspired by gin, whiskey, tequila, triple sec, mezcal, rum, Amaro, Chartreuse, Fernet, Campari, and classic bitters.

I started with gin. It’s complex, interesting, and very drinkable. Bonus: It took just a few hours after gathering everything I needed.

![Image 8: 4 non-alcoholic cocktails with fruit and citrus slices, on a kitchen counter](blob:http://localhost/bbbfda2f776382891d50ccbf603161f3)

Copyright A Bar Above, generated with AI

Most of the whole spices were readily available in the bulk spice section of a gourmet grocery store. A few ingredients– vegetable glycerin and angelica root, specifically– I did have to buy on Amazon.

Zero ABV gin worked well with tonic and as a sour, but I wouldn’t try to tell a gin drinker that it’s gin. In my next batch, I will try to amplify the juniper notes by bruising the juniper berries more.

The recipe cautioned me not to puree the juniper berries, so I may have been too cautious, leaving the tincture lacking the full gin that I enjoy.

![Image 9: 4 non-alcoholic cocktails with fruit and citrus slices, on a kitchen counter](blob:http://localhost/bbbfda2f776382891d50ccbf603161f3)

Copyright A Bar Above, generated with AI

If you go the DIY route, it will help to have a few things on-hand:

*   Blender
*   Digital scales – both a[kitchen scale](https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B01JTDG084?maas=maas_adg_CBBCDB1C46EE1863546805EEDF702D36_afap_abs&ref_=aa_maas) and a [gram scale](https://www.amazon.com/Weigh-Gram-Digital-Jewelry-Kitchen/dp/B06Y61YW7S/ref=sr_1_4?crid=2XRXJIW34HL2C&dchild=1&keywords=gram+scales+digital+weight&qid=1612208454&s=home-garden&sprefix=gram+scale%2Cgarden%2C249&sr=1-4)
*   [Sous vide](https://anovaculinary.com/what-is-sous-vide/)
*   [Juicer](https://www.amazon.com/Extractor-Centrifugal-Vegetable-Anti-drip-Vegetables/dp/B07D3C6NVL/ref=sr_1_3?_encoding=UTF8&c=ts&dchild=1&keywords=Juicers&qid=1612211035&s=kitchen&sr=1-3&ts_id=289926)

Note: The blender and scales are the minimum starting place. You’ll be using your blender to make tinctures (concentrated extracts made by blending up spices, herbs, or barks in a liquid). In the zero ABV gin, I blended juniper berries in a combination of vegetable glycerin and water.

Many of the ingredients you’ll be working with are very aromatic, flavorful, and lightweight, so a little bit will go a long way. Therefore, you’ll be weighing out one to five-gram portions on a gram scale instead of using measuring spoons.

![Image 10: a traditional food scale ](blob:http://localhost/e1d3478b0dad19aa3cdc9d62c5fd01b7)

Photo by Asha Taylor via www.unsplash.com

Water, fruit juice, and vegetable glycerin-heavy ingredients are just too much for the tiny gram scale. That’s why you’ll also need a kitchen scale.

Plus, there are many uses for a scale once it’s part of your kitchen set up: You can weigh flour for baking, sugar and water for making syrups, and food for portion control. What I’m saying is that it’s super handy and you should just get one.

Overall, I’m delighted with the outcome. I know my craft mocktail menu options will be endless when I complete the backbar. Next up is zero ABV American whiskey!

Limitations can inspire creativity. Eliminating alcohol is just such a boundary. Writing this guide to craft mocktails has shown me that complex, well-balanced, and visually stimulating non-alcoholic drinks are more than possible. They are a necessary part of a home bar or professional bar program.

Innovation Investigation: What’s Bubbling Up in Non-Alcoholic Fermented Beverages

Get innovation insights about non-alcoholic fermented beverages like kombucha, kefir, kvass, and tepache that are shaking up the status quo

From tangy sips to probiotic-packed fizz, non-alcoholic fermented beverages deliver a flavorful and functional drinking experience. Although estimates vary, fermented drinks like kombucha, kefir, and kvass may be generating more than $1.1 billion in North America. Forecasts for growth are bullish, with industry watchers predicting that kombucha may have an annual growth rate (CAGR) of 16%, while kefir could generate 4% CAGR over the next five years.

The surge underscores a decisive shift in priorities about [functionality and liquid refreshment](https://flavorsum.com/webcast-bubbling-up-success-in-functional-beverages/). Fermented beverages provide nutrient-rich support for digestive health with a recognized link to boosting immunity. But the bubbly drinks also offer bold, complex flavors with a twist, branching away from standard beverages and offering an exciting dimension to beverage formulation.

We’ve taken a closer look at innovation trends to help you assess the opportunities for beverages shaking up the status quo.

## **A Digestible Explanation of Non-Alcoholic Fermentation**

Fermentation is a process that chemically breaks down organic matter through a kickstart from bacteria, yeasts, or molds. The organisms feed on added sugar, using it as fuel to break down the sweet molecules and convert them into a new form, such as gasses or liquid.

Fermented beverages often start with three ingredients:

5

The mixture changes (ferments) over time, from a few days to almost a month, with the timeline and the base critical elements of getting the desired functional drink.

All fermented drinks produce alcohol as a byproduct of fermentation, but that doesn’t necessarily mean shoppers will need an ID to purchase. Non-alcoholic fermented beverages have shorter fermentation cycles that produce less byproduct. Fermentation times will be longer for beverages with a buzz, like beers, wines, or meads.

## **Non-Alcoholic Fermented Beverages Starting to Pop in North America**

Our innovation investigation examines trends in some of the leading fermented drinks, including kombucha, kefir (dairy-and-water-based), kvass, and fermented juices like tepache.

#### THE RISE AND SPARKLE OF KOMBUCHA

Although kombucha (kuhm BOO chuh) originated centuries ago, the beverage landed in North American grocery stores in the late 90s with the launch of [GT Dave](https://gtslivingfoods.com/pages/about). Now, with more than [650 brands](https://www.boochnews.com/2023/12/07/a-statistical-analysis-of-kombucha-brands-in-the-usa-2020-2023/) available, kombucha has wide market recognition. The fizzy, sour-sweet drink has a fermentation process that often uses a starter culture (SCOBY: Symbiotic Culture of Bacteria and Yeast) in sweetened tea. The resulting base contains vitamins E, K, and B and minerals like potassium and manganese. Kombucha provides developers with a versatile framework for flavors.

Although innovation softened in the most recent year, Mintel reports that about four in ten Americans have tried kombucha, and half would repurchase it. Brands are now creating [hard kombucha](https://www.liquor.com/hard-kombucha-5649374) by extending the fermentation process to boost ABV from less than 0.5% to as high as 9%. Non-alcoholic kombucha producers are finding ways to formulate with less sugar, and the average gr/100ml is 2.3 in 2024, down from more than 3.0 in 2020 (Mintel GNPD).

The beverage is getting more kudos in social discussion for providing convenient, refreshing rejuvenation (Tastewise).

#### KEFIR EXTENDS FROM CREAMY CLASSIC TO A FIZZY FAVORITE

Kefir’s origin story dates back to the [Bronze Age](https://www.culturedfoodlife.com/history-of-kefir-kombucha-and-fermented-vegetables/?srsltid=AfmBOoo2ZGb1exUVGL_Au5KSASeQH633RnipADTgptIC0Tdxgn8B1ea_), making it ‘older’ than Kombucha. The dairy-based fermented beverages started to become mainstream in the late 80s when the [Lifeway](https://lifewaykefir.com/the-world-of-lifeway/) brand launched in North America. [Major brands](https://www.mordorintelligence.com/industry-reports/kefir-market#:~:text=Kefir%20Market%20Leaders-,Lifeway%20Foods%2C%20Inc.,Green%20Valley%20Creamery) began producing kefir, including Hain Celestial, Nestle, Danone, Green Valley Creamery, Maple Hill Creamery, Forager, Redwood Hill Farm & Creamery, Biotiful Dairy, and Emmi AG.

[Dairy-based kefir](https://health.clevelandclinic.org/benefits-of-kefir) (Kuh-FEER) adds kefir milk grains, cauliflower-floret-like pieces containing yeast and microorganisms, to cow, goat, or sheep milk. Although the tart milk drink is akin to drinkable yogurt, kefir has a longer fermentation time, more probiotics, and more effervescence. The fermented beverage provides calcium, magnesium, protein, and vitamins B2, B12, and D. Some brands are incorporating plant-based milk (coconut, cashew, soy, almond, [buckwheat](https://www.foodingredientsfirst.com/video/sial-2024-fermentful-boosts-gut-health-with-flavored-plant-based-kefir.html)) into the fermentation process. Social conversations about dairy-based kefir indicate growing interest, increasing by +10% in the last year.

[Water-based kefir](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2666833522000119#:~:text=it%20seems%20that%20there%20are,War%20was%20over%20in%201855.) dates to the late 1800s and has a water kefir grain (similar in appearance to kefir milk grains) that ferments a sugar-water mixture. Brands are now enhancing Kefir water with additional carbonation and fruit juices or flavor to enhance the fizz and create a soda-like drinking experience. Discussions about kefir soda jumped by 42% in social discussion in the past year.

#### KVASS: A BREAD-TO-BEET PROBIOTIC POWERHOUSE

Kvass (kuh VASS), made from rye bread, barley, or beets left to ferment, has a slightly sour taste and a low alcohol content. Producers often flavor the fermented beverage with mint or fruit like apples, raisins, strawberries, or raspberries. The drink originated in Eastern Europe in the 10th century, arriving in North American grocery stores in 2010 when Coca-Cola brought Krushka & Bochka Kvass to New York. Canadian-based [All Star Beverages](https://allstarsbeverages.com/) continues to expand its kvass distribution.

Like other [functional beverages](https://flavorsum.com/functional-beverages-level-up/), kvass provides more than refreshment, serving up probiotics, vitamin B12, selenium, and manganese. Kvass also contains antioxidants, natural nitrates, vitamins A and C, and potassium. Although few brands currently bottle kvass, the beverage is buzzy in the social landscape, with conversations up by +35% in the last year. [Craft brewers](https://www.insidehook.com/drinks/low-abv-beverage-trend-kvass-making-comeback) are exploring fermented beverages in low-alc and ‘hard’ formulas, getting accolades for sustainability since bread waste is significant in North America.

#### TEPACHE TIME: A SWEET, SPICED TRADITION TAKING FERMENTED BEVERAGES UP A NOTCH

Tepache (te PA che) originated in Mexico in the 15th century when Aztecs created a fermented corn beverage. When the drink traveled north, people changed the base ingredient to pineapple, which has naturally occurring yeasts and microorganisms. The fruit provides a sweeter, fizzier, and more tangy taste experience. Added cinnamon and cloves discourage unwanted organisms from growing in the unpasteurized beverage, and some brands incorporate piloncillo, a flavorful Mexican brown sugar.

[Cans of tepache](https://www.foodandwine.com/game-changers-de-la-calle-tepache-7501799) arrived in North American grocery stores in 2020, and popularity is ramping up, with social discussions increasing by almost 10% in the last year. The soda-like beverage contains probiotics, vitamin C, and bromelain, an enzyme that can help with pain, swelling, and stiffness caused by arthritis. Although the classic tepache has low ABV, some [brewers are raising the alcohol](https://www.drinkcrookedowl.com/post/introducing-crooked-owl-hard-tepache) content to 5% or more.

How to Make Fermented Drinks

Fermented drinks at home: here's what you need to know to start. Save money and improve your health by brewing in your home kitchen.

Make fermented drinks at home. Here’s what you need to know to start. Stop buying store bought kombucha, start saving money and brew these magical elixirs yourself! It’s super easy to make homemade fermented drinks.

I cannot express the depths to which I enjoy making fermented sodas at home. The following text is answers to many common questions that I get. This is real brass tacks information. What I wish to convey here first is how unbelievably satisfying it is to make such a special treat from scratch in your own kitchen. The fast that it takes day or weeks to complete just makes it ever more exciting.

The anticipation when waiting for these ferments to finish, the excitement when popping a top and waiting to see how carbonated it will be. These moments are what we live for here on the Greener Postures Homestead. How satisfying it is to make a drink that I can share with my kids without guilt or worry. Full of real food, probiotics and a very low amount of sugar, I can feel good about sharing these drinks with the whole family.

![Image 1: Fermented jun kombucha in swing top bottles with crushed strawberry and fresh thyme.](https://preservingtoday.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/Strawberry-thyme-jun-kombucha-in-swing-top-bottles-1024x1024.png)

Jun Kombucha flavored with strawberry and thyme, just starting second ferment.

## What are fermented drinks?

Fermented drinks are any beverage made by fermentation. Fermentation is a bacterial process that breaks down carbohydrate and sugar. As a byproduct it creates acids, yeast carbon dioxide and probiotics.

## Are all fermented drinks alcoholic?

No, some fermented drinks are considered to be more like sodas. There is always some alcohol create by the fermentation process, but many recipes can yield negligible amounts of alcohol and be just fine for kids.

Common fermented alcoholic drinks are beer, wine, mead and liquors.

I focus on brewing non-alcoholic drinks in my home. Good stuff the whole family can enjoy.

## What are some nonalcoholic fermented drinks?

I consider nonalcoholic drinks to be fruit kvass, tepache, kombucha, jun, water kefir, ginger beer and root beer. You can also make wild fermented lemonade and any other fruit drink you desire. All these drinks will have at least a trace amount of alcohol. The amount depends on many factors. You can have some control over this if you are making fermented drinks at home.

![Image 2: Gallon jar of kvass fermented drinks.](https://preservingtoday.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/Mango-Kvass-in-gallon-jar-1024x1024.png)

Peach Kvass during first ferment

## Are fermented drinks easy to make at home?

Yes! Many fermented drinks are incredible simple to make. Others are a little more fussy and take extra care. There is a fermented drink for any skill and commitment level.

## What equipment do you need to make fermented drinks at home?

**Equipment:**

All links below are items I own and use to ferment beverages.

*   [gallon size glass jar](https://amzn.to/46iXpa9)
*   [Spoon or ladle](https://amzn.to/3t308Wx)
*   [Measuring cu](https://amzn.to/48lalxK)[ps](https://amzn.to/48lalxK)
*   [Cutting board](https://amzn.to/3rg2f90)

*   [Swing top bottl](https://amzn.to/3PIqXZk)[es](https://amzn.to/3PIqXZk)

## What ingredients do you need to make fermented drinks at home?

The ingredients vary depending on what type of fermented drink you are making. Some fermented drinks take simple ingredients that you likely already have on hand. Others need special starter cultures or SCOBY’s that you can grow or buy from a store. I share some examples below:

*   Water Kefir – [water kefir grains](https://amzn.to/3LmGbjN), sugar, water, fruit or fruit juice (optional)
*   Kombucha – [kombucha SCOBY](https://amzn.to/3rkK6XJ), sugar, black tea, water, fruit or fruit juice (optional)
*   Jun Kombucha – [jun kombucha SCOBY](https://amzn.to/3EINsXw), honey, green tea, water, fruit or fruit juice (optional)
*   Fruit Kvass – water, fruit, sugar
*   Tepache – peel and core of a pineapple, sugar or piloncillo, water, spices (optional)
*   Ginger Beer – ginger, water, sugar, ginger bug starter
*   Root Beer – root beer herbs and spices, sugar, water, ginger bug starter

![Image 3: Fermented drinks root beer and strawberry kvass.](https://preservingtoday.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/09/rootbeer-kvass-and-a-pineapple.jpg)

Root Beer, Strawberry Kvass and a whole pineapple about to become Tepache.

## What directions do you need to follow to make fermented drinks?

The method for making fermented drinks depends on what you’re making. It ranges from extremely simple to somewhat complex.

## How long does it take to ferment a drink?

This also depends on what kind of fermented drink you’re making. Kombucha takes much longer than water kefir or kvass. Kvass can be ready to bottle in just a few days.

Some factors that decide the length of time to ferment a drink is the ambient room temperature in your environment. If your house is very warm, it will ferment faster, if it’s on the cooler side, it will take longer.

The optimal temperature for fermenting kombucha is about 75-85 F . Fermentation won’t occur if it’s too cool. You probably won’ have any luck if it’s 60 F or below.

![Image 4: Fermented peach pom jun kombucha.](https://preservingtoday.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/09/jun-ready-to-drink.jpg)

Peach Pomegranate Jun Kombucha after it’s second ferment, ready to drink!

## What is a perpetual ferment?

I honestly don’t know if anyone else calls it this, but I call certain things _perpetual_ or _rhythm_ ferments. These are the types of drinks or foods that have active cultures or SCOBY’s that you have to feed and care for to keep alive. When your beverages is done, save these cultures and reuse them in a new drink. Well cared for cultures can make an infinite number of batches. It’s like keeping a pet, but unlike a pet it provides you with delicious probiotic rich food and drink.

## What is a SCOBY?

SCOBY stands for Symbiotic Culture of Bacteria and Yeast, and that’s just what it is. These are starter cultures used to make fermented food batch after batch. They are growing, living things. When healthy they will grow and reproduce as they work their magic.

Examples of SCOBY’s are kombucha SCOBY’s and water kefir or milk kefir grains.

![Image 5: Jun kombucha SCOBY starter culture.](https://preservingtoday.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/09/SCOBY.jpg)

A Healthy Jun Kombucha SCOBY (not an alien life form [probably])

## What are kefir grains?

Kefir grains can refer to water kefir or [milk kefir grains](https://amzn.to/44XQpOy). These SCOBY’s are small and look a bit like jelly or cottage cheese. You can strain them and reuse them in new ferments. They need to be fed and cared for, when they are they will grow and thrive.

## Are fermented drinks carbonated?

Carbon dioxide is a natural byproduct of the fermentation process. Fortunately for us, we can use this byproduct to make a delicious fizzy drink. By trapping the c02 into a bottle and letting it build up you can yield a yummy effervescent soda. That is natural carbonation.

On the flip side, if you trap in too much c02 you can end up with a foamy mess when you open your bottle. Even worse yet, you could end up with an exploding glass bottle. That is why it’s important to make sure any swing top bottles you buy are fermentation grade. Fermentation grade glass bottles are designed to hold more pressure.

My favorite way to avoid soda eruptions is to use the plastic bottle method for my secondary ferment.

![Image 6: Fermented drinks raspberry kvass.](https://preservingtoday.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/09/strawberry-kvass-1024x1024.jpg)

## What is the plastic bottle method?

Plastic bottle method just means to use a plastic bottle for the secondary ferment. Basically I just strain some of the drink into a plastic bottle. This plastic bottle will act as my gauge to see how much pressure is building up during the secondary fermentation process.

Give a plastic bottle a little squeeze and you will see that it has some give. When you start to feel the bottle is tight, it’s time to move your bottles of fermented drinks into the fridge.

You can use any plastic bottle. Usually I buy a plain sparking water in a 16 oz bottle and safe that. I only use one and bottle the rest in glass. I use the plastic one as the gauge for all the bottles. If they are all the same size, with the same contents and same conditions one bottle should work for keeping an eye on all of them.

## What is secondary fermentation?

Secondary fermentation, second ferment or sometimes called 2F is the step in making fermented beverages where you strain your liquid and move it into a sealed bottle. This is the time you can flavor your drink with crushed fruit, herbs or juice. After it’s bottles it will continue to sit at room temperature to build up carbonation. That is the second ferment.

![Image 7: golden beet kvass](https://preservingtoday.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/09/golden-beet-kvass.jpg)

## Are fermented drinks high in sugar?

The absolute best part about making fermented soda at home is that you have control over how much and what goes into your brew. The sugar in my homemade drinks are a fraction of anything you can buy at the store.

The amount of sugar in a finished ferment is less than what goes into the bottle. That’s because the fermentation process metabolizes sugars and converts them into acids. By fermenting your beverage, you are reducing the overall amount of sugar in your drinks.

The longer you ferment a drink, the less sugary and more acidic it becomes. You can ferment kombucha for just a week or 10 days, or you can let it go for 20-30 days. What you end up with as you final product will be wildly different. One tasting more sweet and they other more sour and vinegary.

## In conclusion

Fermented drinks are sodas that you can make at home with simple real food ingredients. They are full of probiotics, vitamins and minerals and relatively low in sugar.

If you are looking for a alternative to conventional store bought sodas or big brand kombuchas, getting started with making fermented beverages at home is a great option.

Molecular Mixology: What To Know

Molecular mixology is the latest trend in bartending right now, but what is it and what are molecular mixology techniques? Discover it all here...

In the world of bartending, molecular mixology is a rather strange concept. Molecular cocktails are not like any of the classic cocktails, they’re specially made with special pieces of special equipment.

But what is molecular mixology and how do you make a molecular cocktail?

## **What is molecular mixology?**

Molecular mixology is a type of bartending, in which a number of processes and techniques are used, reminiscent to that of a science lesson.

Molecular mixology involves using professional equipment like blowtorches, liquid nitrogen, foams and mists. These kits enhance the cocktail by creating new flavours and sensations. Using this equipment when creating molecular cocktails also means that you’ll be creating an amazing visual effect.

For many, molecular mixology may add to the performance element of bartending that many enjoy, while for others it offers an insight into the inner-workings of drink-making processes and mixology.

## **Molecular mixology techniques**

![Image 1: Molecular cocktail with smoke](https://barschool.b-cdn.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/resized-image-Promo-2022-08-25T131812.191.jpeg)

Molecular mixologists use a whole range of techniques and ingredients when creating a molecular cocktail. Below are some of the most common techniques in molecular mixology…

### Spherification

As a technique borrowed from molecular gastronomy, spherification is the process that enables liquid to form into gelatinous spheres, similar to fish eggs. This effect is made possible by taking a liquid that contains no calcium and mixing it with sodium alginate, then adding this in small amounts to a liquid diluted with calcium chloride. All together they work as gelling agents.

An example of a cocktail made using this technique could be the Molecular [Mojito](https://www.barschool.net/recipes/mojito), which can be made by adding 1.25ml calcium lactate with fresh lime juice, sugar syrup and mint leaves before muddling, and then adding rum and soda water. After pouring the solution (without adding ice) into ice cube trays and freezing, the frozen Mojito cubes should be dropped into a large glass with sodium alginate dissolved in water, and left for 15 minutes. The mojito spheres should be washed in a container of clean water, then they are ready as curious cocktail balls.

### Emulsification

Another concept common to molecular mixology and molecular gastronomy is emulsification.

This involves the binding together of two liquids that don’t usually mix, through the use of an emulsifier. In this way, fats can be used in cocktails where they would usually naturally separate. By using an emulsifier, (such as Ticaloid 210S) a combination of gum acacia and xanthan gum can be used to make the Cold Buttered Rum cocktail. Rum and lime juice are mixed together with butter syrup, a sweet, creamy fusion that would otherwise be impossible to achieve. The result is a lovely smooth molecular cocktail!

### Suspension

Xanthan gum can also be used for another technique called ‘suspension’. The gum can be used to stabilise and thicken a liquid. The flavour is not unpleasant, so it can be useful for bartenders when creating drinks like Sangria, where the ingredients appear suspended in motion when viewed through the glass.

### Hot infusion siphon

For the customer that enjoys being involved in the drinks-making process, the hot infusion siphon can be just the thing. This table-top infusion apparatus allows the drinker to watch the infusion process as it happens, and enjoy the result.

It requires water, sugar syrup and a base spirit, such as gin, in the lower chamber. Whilst the ingredients to be infused sit in the upper chamber, such as lemongrass, lavender or jasmine. When the infusion has finished, the warm cocktail can be poured into a glass and enjoyed. Hot infusion siphons are usually commonplace in molecular mixology kits.

There a whole host of other techniques and equipment used in molecular mixology like liquid nitrogen to make dry ice and loads of other gelling agents and gums. Molecular mixologists essentially work in a science lab behind the bar.

Molecular mixology isn’t just making cocktails, it’s making a molecular cocktail through crazy processes and molecular equipment! If you’re a lover of mixology, you’ll definitely love molecular mixology.

## **History of molecular mixology**

Molecular mixology is a derivation of the term ‘molecular gastronomy’ coined in 1988, which entails using similar scientific effects but in the kitchen.

Taxonomy aside, as the inventor of the flaming Blue Blazer it could be said that the godfather of bartending, Jerry Thomas, was the original molecular mixologist, all the way from the nineteenth century. Thomas was certainly a man ahead of his time, and while there have been more flaming and frozen effects in the meantime, for the most part it has taken a full century for any real developments to take place in this area of bartending.

Thankfully, the last two decades have been witness to some astonishing progress in conjuring tricks and concoctions behind the bar, and with technology advancing fast it would seem that more is still to come.

 Turn a classic cocktail into a molecular one, through graduating as a professional bartender with one of our [bartending courses](https://www.barschool.net/courses).

molecular mixology | The Oxford Companion to Spirits & Cocktails

is the popular term for the application of modern scientific investigation, knowledge, tools, substances, and processes to the creation and production of cocktails, usually with a

is the popular term for the application of modern scientific investigation, knowledge, tools, substances, and processes to the creation and production of cocktails, usually with a goal of creating an effect that is unobtainable or impracticable using traditional means and methods. Depending on the intentions and aesthetic of the creator, cocktails produced by these methods may be whimsical or challenging in form and/or context or may be broadly similar to traditional cocktails.

The name derives from the so-called molecular gastronomy or modernist cuisine culinary movement as investigated, practiced, and documented by Hervé This, Ferran Adrià, Heston Blumenthal, Nathan Myhrvold, and others and frequently utilizes ingredients, equipment, and techniques pioneered in that movement. Some influential bartenders in this style are Dave Arnold, Eben Freeman, and Eben Klemm in New York, Tony Conigliaro in London, and Jamie Boudreau in Seattle, Washington.

Representative tools, techniques, and ingredients used by molecular mixology bartenders include the following:

### Additives

Bartenders avail themselves of the full range of food-safe chemicals and other additives to produce specific results unobtainable or impracticable by other means. For example, citric and other acids can be used to adjust the sourness of fruit juices; sodium bisulfite helps to preserve the color of green juices; and liquid-filled spheres are created using sodium citrate, sodium alginate, calcium chloride, calcium lactate, and/or calcium lactate gluconate.

### Barrel Aging

A cocktail is created in sufficient volume to fill a wooden cask and subsequently aged for a period of time in it. When the desired result is obtained, the barrel-aged cocktail is decanted into a nonreactive vessel for storage and service. The type of wood, size, age, preparation, and previous use of the cask, as well as the length of aging, all influence the results of the barrel-aging process. This technique is primarily used for cocktails such as the Negroni or Manhattan that have an inherently strong flavor and do not contain fresh ingredients.

### Carbonation

Carbon dioxide is dissolved into one or more components of a cocktail at high pressure in order to produce an effervescent beverage. Alternatively, fruit may be infused with carbon dioxide in order to create garnish that effervesces as it is eaten. Carbonation produces a characteristic “prickling” sensation in the mouth as the cocktail is consumed, and the carbon dioxide that is released can have a significant impact on perceived flavor as a result of the way it affects retronasal olfaction, the process in which odor molecules pass upward from the oral cavity to olfactory receptors in the back of the nasal cavity.

### Clarification

Ingredients such as fresh juices are clarified to produce transparent and frequently colorless liquids having the desirable flavors and other characteristics of the original ingredient. Common clarification techniques employed in molecular mixology include enzymatic degradation, fining, and centrifuging, often in combination. Another popular process is to add gelatin or agar-agar to a liquid, which is subsequently frozen and thawed, trapping unwanted particulate matter in the semisolid matrix that is left behind. Each method of clarification has a different yield and effect on the resultant clarified liquid and may be better suited to particular liquids or contemplated uses. Decolored clarified liquids allow bartenders to produce cocktails with unexpected flavors due to the absence of familiar visual cues, and the removal of suspended particles makes it possible to carbonate beverages containing clarified fresh juices.

### Edible Cocktails

Various methods can be employed to produce a solid food otherwise having the flavors and alcoholic content of a cocktail. Some well-known examples of edible cocktails include marshmallows, sorbets, breakfast cereal, gelatin in various shapes, and vacuum-infused fruits or vegetables such as cucumbers.

### Fat Washing

This traditional perfumer’s technique takes advantage of the fact that most fat-soluble substances are also soluble in alcohol. An aromatic and flavorful fat is combined with a spirit and allowed to rest; then, after the infusion is complete, the mixture is chilled until the fat solidifies and can be strained off. Fat washing has been used to flavor spirits with bacon fat, brown butter, cheese, extra virgin olive oil, duck fat, peanut butter, and chorizo fat, to name a few well-known examples.

### Foams

Flavorful liquids are combined with ingredients such as gelatin, lecithin, agar-agar, egg whites, egg white powder, and gum arabic, and air or gas is incorporated to create bubbles. Depending on the ingredients and techniques employed, the foam can be wet or dry, stiff or loose, and having fine or large bubbles. Foams are not typically complete cocktails in and of themselves but are usually layered over a liquid to contribute a contrasting aroma, flavor, and/or texture component.

### Gels and Gums

Spirits and other ingredients are combined with a gelling agent such as gelatin or agar-agar, then allowed to set. The gels can be garnished and consumed as an edible cocktail, or they can be used as a garnish or semisolid component in a liquid cocktail.

### Liquid Nitrogen

This super-cold liquid is −195.79° C and is used in a variety of innovative and interesting ways in the production of cocktails. For example, green herbs such as mint or basil can be frozen to a very low temperature with liquid nitrogen, shattered into tiny pieces, and combined with spirits to result in an extra-strong herbal extraction without any of the off-flavors normally associated with enthusiastic muddling and oxidation. Liquid nitrogen can be poured onto the surface of a cocktail to create a frozen layer over which other liquids will be added, or spirits may be mixed with liquid nitrogen in order to produce a frozen “cocktail sorbet.” Bartenders with ready access to liquid nitrogen also find it convenient for chilling glassware. Special care must be taken when working with liquid nitrogen, as improper use can lead to tissue damage from freezing, asphyxiation from vaporized nitrogen, and even explosions resulting from pressure buildup in unsuitable storage vessels.

### Spherification

Various chemicals and techniques are used to create liquid-filled spheres ranging in size from caviar to egg yolks, which are then served as an edible cocktail or used as a component in a liquid cocktail. As the spheres rupture and release their liquid contents in the mouth, they create “bursts” of flavor that, in a liquid cocktail, enhance, alter, or contrast with the primary flavors. Especially popular as a garnish for champagne, spherification has been one of the most widespread techniques of molecular mixology, to such an extent that the company Rémy Cointreau created a special kit with all the ingredients and equipment for making “Cointreau pearls.”

### Sous Vide

In molecular mixology this technique is primarily used for infusions and takes advantage of one of the primary techniques and equipment sets of molecular gastronomy. Spirits or other liquids are sealed in a plastic pouch or other airtight container together with a flavoring agent such as tea, fresh or dried herbs or spices, fruits, or vegetables. The container is then placed in a temperature-controlled water bath, heated for a period of time, and then chilled and strained. Sous vide techniques allow for precisely controlled infusions and extraction of flavors that would be impossible or impracticable using traditional means. The chamber vacuum machine, a common piece of equipment employed in sous vide techniques, can also be used to quickly infuse porous fruits and vegetables with spirits or other liquids. Although vacuum packaging for culinary use may be highly scrutinized and tightly regulated in some jurisdictions, a jar or bottle serves as well as a vacuum bag for most applications of this technique that have relevance to molecular mixology.

### Vacuum Distillation

A piece of laboratory equipment called a rotary evaporator is used to perform distillations at low temperatures by reducing gas pressure. This technology makes it possible to concentrate flavors, extract essential oils, and produce uniquely flavored liquids with high precision and without altering or damaging fresh flavors with heat. Vacuum distillation has been used to concentrate fruit juices, extract aromas from unlikely substances such as leather or soil, remove oak byproducts from barrel-aged spirits, create chile-flavored spirits without spicy capsaicin and tea-flavored spirits without astringent tannins, produce water-based distillations called hydrosols using delicate flowers or herbs, and in the creation of many other products used by molecular mixologists. Although the alcohol-based products are some of the more dramatic and popular vacuum distillates for demonstration purposes, they are illegal to serve in most countries around the world. It is also illegal in many jurisdictions to possess distilling equipment and/or perform distillations of any kind on-premises without a permit. As a result, drinks containing vacuum-distilled components are rarely encountered in a commercial setting.

### Here's how to master at-home clarification, fermentation, force carbonation and more.

Like any practice, there are levels to at-home bartending. Stocking up on the [best tools](https://punchdrink.com/articles/ultimate-home-bar-accessories-guide/), [spirits for mixing](https://punchdrink.com/articles/best-well-liquors-bartenders/) and [classic recipes](https://punchdrink.com/articles/ultimate-best-classic-cocktail-recipes-old-fashioned-negroni-margarita/) may be one tier of mastery, but building an entire carbonation rig in your kitchen is probably the ultimate home bar flex. If you’ve nailed the [easy cocktail projects](https://punchdrink.com/articles/easy-cocktail-projects-techniques/), it’s time to take things up a notch. Here are five next-level cocktail projects to try.

###### [Fat-Washing](https://punchdrink.com/articles/how-to-fat-wash-cocktail-recipes-with-bacon-milk-washing-effleurage/)

First employed in the famous[Benton’s Old-Fashioned](https://punchdrink.com/recipes/bentons-old-fashioned/) at PDT in 2007, fat-washing has evolved to encompass a whole wave of spirit-infusion techniques. At its simplest, fat-washing requires melting a fat—say, coconut oil or animal fat—infusing it into a spirit, freezing the mixture, then straining out the solids for a bolder, fuller-bodied flavor. Try the technique with [coconut oil](https://punchdrink.com/recipes/bikini-martini/), [chile oil](https://punchdrink.com/recipes/lucy-liu/) and even [peanut butter](https://punchdrink.com/recipes/romance-in-graceland/).

###### [Clarification](https://punchdrink.com/articles/clarified-milk-punch-techniques-recipes/)

Transform everything from [Daiquiris](https://punchdrink.com/recipes/groove-in-the-heart/) to [Cuba Libres](https://punchdrink.com/recipes/sex-panther/) into crystal-clear liquid—no centrifuge necessary—with one of [several techniques](https://punchdrink.com/articles/clarified-milk-punch-techniques-recipes/): Allow the solids within a cocktail to gel with the addition of agar-agar before straining them out; curdle them with milk, as is often seen in clarified milk punches; or simply filter out those particles with a sieve or muslin.

###### [Fermentation](https://punchdrink.com/articles/drink-science-team-lyan-how-to-ferment-drinks-at-home-fermented-cocktails-recipe/)

Fermentation projects shouldn’t be relegated to sourdough starters and pickles. Equipped with a packet of wine yeast, you can transform teas, juices or jams into [wine-like ferment](https://punchdrink.com/articles/drink-science-team-lyan-how-to-ferment-drinks-at-home-fermented-cocktails-recipe/). The final product can be treated as a finished cocktail or mixed with other ingredients to enhance the complexity of even the simplest formula. Try [lacto-fermenting cherries](https://punchdrink.com/recipes/windowsill-thief/) for syrups and garnishes, [celery soda](https://punchdrink.com/recipes/cel-rey/) to top mezcal highballs or [raspberry cordial](https://punchdrink.com/recipes/amaro-kalimotxo/) for an elevated Kalimotxo.

[According to Jack Schramm](https://punchdrink.com/articles/maximalists-guide-to-force-carbonated-cocktails/), a highball is never just two ingredients—that is, if you consider that carbonation is an ingredient unto itself. To unlock the best highballs, bartenders turn to force carbonation, a technique that creates better, longer-lasting bubbles. [This Frankenstein approach to spirit infusion](https://punchdrink.com/articles/goodbye-fat-washing-hello-switching-spirit-infusion-cocktail-technique/) requires freezing the spirit’s water content to separate it from the alcohol, then replacing it with just about any liquid. Ia i n McPherson, one of the primary advocates of the technique, has experimented with grapefruit gin and watermelon bourbon. So long as you have a freezer that can reach –27ºC (–17°F), there’s plenty of room for experimentation.
